Quantum Capital: an interactive brief

⬇ Download the data (xlsx)
Developed by Ron Nodel (UCLA) with Avasant · rnodel@g.ucla.edu
Method: click to expand
What this is. Every financing event and government program in the quantum computing industry that could be verified, 2002–2026. The download button above gives you the full dataset. Building and checking it took 2,449 research agents and ≈4.9 billion tokens of analysis.

Why it can be trusted. Every figure traces to a primary source in two clicks, and every number passed two independent verification stages, the second forbidden to confirm using the source the first one found. That second stage overturned or withdrew 37 of the last 72 figures it examined, including several of our own. Amounts are what actually reached the company, net of fees and redemptions, never the headline. Where a figure could not be verified it is left out and the gap is stated rather than filled with an estimate.

What this does not cover. This tracks capital that companies raise. Several of the largest quantum programs in the world raise nothing publicly known, so no amount is recorded for them: Google, Microsoft, Intel, Amazon, NVIDIA, IBM outside its government awards, NTT, Hitachi, Toshiba and Fujitsu all fund quantum from internal budgets that no filing separates from the rest of the business. They appear in the company lists, and they appear when they transact externally through government awards, acquisitions, and investments they make in others. Their internal spending is real and is not counted, because estimating it would mean inventing a number. China's state spending is excluded for the same reason. National program budgets are tracked separately in figure 3 rather than mixed into company capital.

How every number was checked: two independent steps.
1 · A research agent finds the figure in a primary source: an SEC or stock-exchange filing, a government award database, or the company's own announcement. 2 · A second, independent agent tries to refute it: re-deriving the amount at fixed exchange rates and testing it against every other event for double-counting. Only figures that survive both steps are shown. What counts as money. Cash that actually reached the company: after share redemptions, after fees. Announced headlines are not used: a "$400M" listing that delivered $96M after redemptions is shown as $96M. Program budgets ("up to $X") are never mixed into company capital. They are spread across their official spend periods and shown as their own series in figure 3, and figure 2's government band is the sum of that series and the money paid direct to companies.

Known limits, stated plainly. 216 of 975 events have undisclosed amounts, so every total is a minimum. Government awards to companies in 2014–2019 are under-counted (US award databases limited access during collection). China's state spending is excluded as unquantifiable; disclosed Chinese company raises are included.

Coverage. To our knowledge this is the most comprehensive publicly available database of quantum companies and their financing: 975 events across 272 funded companies and roughly 450 tracked in total, 89 national programs, 2002 to August 2026, every figure carrying its source.
